name: scheme48
why: A compact Scheme byte-code interpreter with a long research lineage, a good door into Scheme implementation internals.

brief.what_it_is: Scheme 48 is an implementation of the Scheme programming language built on a byte-code interpreter. The homepage describes it as a testbed for implementation techniques and as an expository tool, which makes it a window into how a Scheme system is built. The homepage does not say what input it reads or what output it produces beyond running Scheme programs. The Homebrew metadata lists four executables: scheme48, scheme48-config, scheme-r5rs, and scheme-srfi-7. The homepage also links a manual in HTML, PDF, and PostScript forms.
brief.why_it_exists: Written by Richard Kelsey and Jonathan Rees, it is meant to be a testbed for experiments in implementation techniques and an expository tool. The homepage frames it as a research and teaching vehicle rather than a production product.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says it is based on a byte-code interpreter. It does not explain the mechanism further. The homepage also says Pre-Scheme, a statically typed Scheme dialect used to implement Scheme 48's own virtual machine, originated with this project.
brief.install_notes: The homepage links a source distribution for 1.9.3 and a Windows distribution, but the Windows link is labelled 1.9 rather than 1.9.3. Building from development sources is described on a separate page that I did not follow. Beyond brew install, I did not see configuration or first-run steps.
brief.standout: The project doubles as a research testbed and an expository tool, and it is the implementation language basis for Pre-Scheme, which is used to write its own virtual machine. It also spawned related systems: Kali, a distributed Scheme, and scsh, a scripting and systems environment built on top of it.
brief.status: Maintained as of the homepage: current release 1.9.3 dated November 2024, with release notes and a manual on the site. I did not check the commit history or a repository, so I cannot say more about recent activity.
brief.caveats: The homepage gives no install or build instructions beyond pointing at a separate build page that I did not open. The Windows distribution is listed as 1.9, not 1.9.3, so it may lag the current release. I did not check licensing. Homebrew's caveats field is empty.
quotes: Scheme 48 is an implementation of Scheme written by Richard Kelsey and Jonathan Rees.
It is based on a byte-code interpreter and is designed to be used as a testbed for experiments in implementation techniques and as an expository tool.

Pre-Scheme is a statically typed dialect of the Scheme programming language, combining the flexibility of Scheme with the efficiency and low-level machine access of C, which originated with Scheme 48, where it is used to implement its virtual machine.
fetch_log: https://www.s48.org/ — fetched OK; homepage text read. Link targets for release notes, source, manual, and development pages were not exposed in the returned text, so I did not follow them. Stopped at one fetch.

judge.reason: Scheme 48 is more than another interpreter: its Pre-Scheme dialect implements its bytecode VM, making it an unusually tangible doorway into language-runtime design.

entry.title: Scheme 48
entry.tldr: A Scheme interpreter built on a byte-code VM, made by Kelsey and Rees as a testbed and teaching tool, and the birthplace of Pre-Scheme.
entry.deeper_look:
Scheme 48 is an implementation of the Scheme language written by Richard Kelsey and Jonathan Rees. It runs Scheme programs on a byte-code interpreter. The homepage describes it as "a testbed for experiments in implementation techniques and as an expository tool", so it is meant to be read and studied as well as run.

The idea underneath is that a language system can be small enough to understand. Scheme 48's virtual machine is not written in C by hand. It is written in Pre-Scheme, "a statically typed dialect of the Scheme programming language, combining the flexibility of Scheme with the efficiency and low-level machine access of C". Pre-Scheme originated here, so the system is partly written in a dialect of the language it implements.

The project also led to related systems: Kali, a distributed Scheme, and scsh, a scripting and systems environment built on top of it. The homepage links a manual in HTML, PDF and PostScript. Homebrew installs four executables: scheme48, scheme48-config, scheme-r5rs and scheme-srfi-7.

entry.whats_unique: It is a Scheme built to be studied, with a VM written in Pre-Scheme, a dialect that began in this very project. It is also the base that scsh and Kali were built on.
entry.caveats: The brief found no first-run steps beyond installing, so expect to read the manual on the homepage to get going.
